# 2 Kings Chapter 18 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 239r–240v | **Source Image:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/2KI_018_page_476.jpg, 2KI_018_page_477.jpg, 2KI_018_page_478.jpg, 2KI_018_page_479.jpg

---

**1** In the third year of Hoshea son of Elah, king of Israel, Hezekiah son of Ahaz became king of Judah.

**2** He was twenty-five when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for twenty-nine years. His mother was Abi, daughter of Zechariah.

**3** He did what was right in the LORD's eyes, just as his ancestor David had done.

**4** He tore down the high places, smashed the sacred pillars, and cut down the Asherah pole. He also broke into pieces the bronze snake Moses had made, because the Israelites had been burning incense to it up to that time. He called it Nehushtan — "just a piece of bronze."

**5** Hezekiah trusted in the LORD, the God of Israel. There was no king like him among all the kings of Judah — not before him and not after him.

**6** He held fast to the LORD and never stopped following him. He obeyed the commands the LORD had given through Moses.

**7** The LORD was with him, and he succeeded in everything he undertook. He rebelled against the king of Assyria and refused to serve him.

**8** He defeated the Philistines as far as Gaza and its surrounding territory, from the smallest outpost to the largest fortified city.

**9** In Hezekiah's fourth year — the seventh year of Hoshea son of Elah king of Israel — King Shalmaneser of Assyria marched against Samaria and laid siege to it.

**10** After three years, the Assyrians captured it. So Samaria fell in Hezekiah's sixth year, Hoshea's ninth year.

**11** The king of Assyria deported the Israelites to Assyria and resettled them in Halah, along the Habor River in the region of Gozan, and in the cities of the Medes.

**12** This happened because they had not obeyed the LORD their God. They had violated his covenant — everything Moses, the LORD's servant, had commanded. They refused to listen or obey.

**13** In Hezekiah's fourteenth year, King Sennacherib of Assyria attacked all the fortified cities of Judah and captured them.

**14** Hezekiah sent a message to the king of Assyria at Lachish: "I have done wrong. Withdraw from me, and I will pay whatever you demand." The king of Assyria demanded three hundred talents of silver and thirty talents of gold.

**15** So Hezekiah handed over all the silver found in the LORD's temple and in the royal treasury.

**16** He even stripped the gold from the temple doors and doorposts — gold he himself had put there — and gave it to the king of Assyria.

**17** Despite this, the king of Assyria sent his supreme commander, his chief officer, and his chief negotiator from Lachish to Jerusalem with a massive army. They marched up and took position near the aqueduct of the Upper Pool, on the road to the Washerman's Field.

**18** They called for the king, and three officials came out to meet them: Eliakim son of Hilkiah, the palace administrator; Shebna the court secretary; and Joah son of Asaph, the royal herald.

**19** The Rabshakeh said to them, "Give Hezekiah this message from the great king, the king of Assyria: What makes you so confident?

**20** You talk about having strategy and military strength — but these are just empty words. Who are you really counting on, that you dare rebel against me?

**21** Look — you're leaning on Egypt, a splintered walking stick! If you lean on it, it drives into your hand and pierces it. That's what Pharaoh king of Egypt is to everyone who relies on him.

**22** And if you tell me, 'We are trusting in the LORD our God' — isn't he the one whose shrines and altars Hezekiah has torn down? Hezekiah told Judah and Jerusalem, 'You must worship only at this altar in Jerusalem.'

**23** Come now — let's make a bet with my master the king of Assyria. I'll give you two thousand horses if you can find enough riders to put on them!

**24** You can't even repulse a single minor officer from my master's forces. And you're counting on Egypt for chariots and cavalry?

**25** Besides — do you think I've marched against this place without the LORD's approval? The LORD himself told me, 'March against this land and destroy it.'"

**26** Then Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah said to the Rabshakeh, "Please — speak to us in Aramaic. We understand it. Don't speak to us in Hebrew where the people on the wall can hear."

**27** But the Rabshakeh replied, "Do you think my master sent me to say these things only to you and your master? My message is for those men sitting on the wall — the ones who will be eating their own filth and drinking their own urine along with you!"

**28** Then the Rabshakeh stood up and shouted in Hebrew at the top of his voice: "Listen to the message of the great king, the king of Assyria!

**29** The king says: Don't let Hezekiah fool you. He cannot rescue you from my power.

**30** Don't let Hezekiah talk you into trusting the LORD by saying, 'The LORD will certainly rescue us — this city will never fall to the king of Assyria.'

**31** Don't listen to Hezekiah! This is what the king of Assyria says: Make peace with me and surrender. Then each of you can eat from your own grapevine and your own fig tree, and drink water from your own well,

**32** until I come to resettle you in a land just like yours — a land of grain and wine, bread and vineyards, olive groves and honey. Choose life, not death! Don't listen to Hezekiah — he's misleading you when he says, 'The LORD will rescue us.'

**33** Has any god of any nation ever rescued his people from the king of Assyria?

**34** Where are the gods of Hamath and Arpad? Where are the gods of Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivvah? Did they rescue Samaria from my power?

**35** Name one god among all the gods of these lands who has rescued his country from me. What makes you think the LORD can rescue Jerusalem?"

**36** The people on the wall stayed completely silent. No one said a word, because the king had ordered, "Do not answer him."

**37** Then Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah went to Hezekiah with their clothes torn in grief and reported everything the Rabshakeh had said.

---
## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

**Verse 4 — Nehushtan:** This is one of the bravest acts of any king in the Bible. The bronze serpent was made by Moses himself — it had genuine sacred history behind it (Numbers 21). But when a sacred object becomes an idol, it must be destroyed. Hezekiah smashes it and gives it a mocking name: *Nehushtan* — a pun meaning roughly "bronze-thing" or "snake-thing." He reduces a centuries-old relic to scrap metal with a nickname. This is what real reform looks like: it costs something.

**Verse 5 — "no king like him":** The narrator gives Hezekiah the highest possible praise. But the same words will be said of Josiah later (23:25). This is not a contradiction — it is a deliberate pairing. Hezekiah excels in *trust* (the key word of this chapter); Josiah excels in *obedience*. Together they represent the complete ideal.

**Verse 19-35 — The Rabshakeh's speech:** This is the most sophisticated piece of psychological warfare in the Bible. The Rabshakeh systematically demolishes every source of Judean confidence: (1) Egypt is useless (v.21); (2) YHWH has been alienated by Hezekiah's own reforms (v.22); (3) Judah has no military strength (vv.23-24); (4) YHWH himself authorized Assyria's attack (v.25); (5) no god has ever stopped Assyria (vv.33-35). The speech is delivered in Hebrew, not Aramaic — deliberately aimed at the common people on the wall, not the diplomats. The Rabshakeh is trying to break the city's will before a single arrow is fired.

**Verse 36 — Silence:** The people's silence is one of the most powerful moments in Kings. They have just heard the most devastating argument against their faith — and they say nothing. Not because they agree, but because the king told them not to answer. Their obedience to Hezekiah in this moment is itself an act of trust.

*— PNEUMA*
